title: Slip, Trip and Fall Prevention
summary: Same-level falls start with debris, nails, waste, and slippery or uneven stairs. OSHA's housekeeping and stairway rules give the basics for keeping walking surfaces safe.
talking_points: Keep form and scrap lumber with protruding nails, and all other debris, cleared from work areas, passageways and stairs (29 CFR 1926.25(a)).
Remove combustible scrap and debris at regular intervals, and provide a safe way to do it (1926.25(b)).
Use containers to collect waste, trash, oily rags and refuse. Containers for oily, flammable or hazardous waste need covers and must be emptied at frequent and regular intervals (1926.25(c)).
Stairways must be free of hazardous projections such as protruding nails (1926.1052(a)(6)).
Slippery conditions on stairways must be eliminated before the stairs are used (1926.1052(a)(7)).
Riser height and tread depth must be uniform within a flight of stairs, with no more than 1/4 inch of variation in any stairway system (1926.1052(a)(3)).
Stairways with four or more risers, or rising more than 30 inches, need at least one handrail (1926.1052(c)(1)(i)).
Good practice: clean up a spill or clear debris the moment you see it, and tell the crew if you cannot fix it right away.
site_hazards_to_check: Debris or materials in walkways, passageways and stairs
Wet, muddy or icy stairs and walking surfaces
Stair risers or treads that are not uniform
Stairways with no handrail where one is required
discussion_questions: Where on this site are people most likely to trip, and who is responsible for clearing it?
What do you do when you find a slippery or damaged stair you cannot fix yourself?
How often is scrap removed from our work area?

flags: Verified 1926.25(a)-(c) and 1926.1052(a)(3),(a)(6),(a)(7),(c)(1)(i) verbatim on osha.gov; the 1/4 inch and four-risers/30-inch figures match.
